lessons.title: hablan — "they speak," and "you all speak"
lessons.gloss: they speak" — and, across most of the Spanish-speaking world, "you all speak

segments.text: Say "we speak." (Hablamos.) And what was the form for he speaks? (Habla.)
Take habla, the form for one other person, and add -n:
That is the whole operation, and it is the same one Spanish uses everywhere: a final -n on a verb means the subject is plural and is not you.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the form does a second job, exactly as habla did

segments.text: ustedes — you all. And it takes hablan, the they form.

You have seen this exact move before. Usted takes the he/she form because it grew out of vuestra merced, "your grace" — a thing you talk about. Ustedes is simply that phrase made plural, vuestras mercedes, "your graces". Same origin, same consequence.

Where this is the ordinary word. Across all of Latin America, and in the Canary Islands and parts of Andalusia, ustedes is how you address any group — friends, family, strangers alike. There is no separate familiar plural. For most Spanish speakers alive, this lesson is the complete answer to "how do I talk to more than one person?"
Spain uses a different word for friends, and it has the next chapter to itself.

segments.instruction: "habla" then "hablan" — one other person, then several

feedback.correct: Yes — ustedes takes the they form, for the same reason usted takes the he form.

segments.prompt: What phrase is ustedes worn down from?

feedback.correct: Yes — your graces, the plural of the phrase behind usted.

segments.text: What is "they speak"? (Hablan.) What does a final -n on a verb tell you? (The subject is plural, and not you.) And who does ustedes address in Latin America? (Any group at all.) Next: the word Spain uses instead, for friends.
